items.summary: Editorial arguing that the club lacks team spirit outside the walkers, pointing to Linda Nicholls' Swedish trip and Arnold Bentt's jumpers as examples, and urging training trips and a continental holiday for the young athletes.
items.text:
"The team that trains together stays together": a statement that contains more than a little truth. Our walkers are small in numbers but they have a closely knit fraternity that goes hand in hand with success. Our runners, meanwhile, have not been successful since the 60's and although laudable attempts have been made to foster the pack training system, with due respect, it is not the 'A' team runners who have responded. Track and field tends to be even more individualistic and true to form, our track men rarely even see each other apart from match days; the social event of the year is a quick drink together after our single home league fixture. Not surprising then that when the result sheets are handed out Belgrave Harriers features a little lower down the list than we would like.

We do have a problem in that our membership is drawn from a large catchment area and this is further aggravated by our head-quarters being ten miles from our track base but more could be done to engender a sense of togetherness or team spirit, call it what you will.

Linda Nicholls writes in this issue of her stay with a Swedish club which regularly goes out into the countryside to camp and train together. Arnold Bentt, in "Spotlight", harks back to the days when we had a group of successful jumpers all working at their events together. The lesson seems obvious.

At present we have a fine bunch of young athletes who should go far if we can only keep them together. So let's liven things up a bit, plan a few training trips, and what about an athletic holiday on the Continent next year. Or are we all too old and staid and unable to climb out of the rut?

items.heading: grapevine
items.summary: Grapevine column of club news and gossip.
items.text:
We are sorry to report that Gordon Doubleday, a key member of the "Belgravian" team, has had a spell in Kingston Hospital thanks to a recurrence of the heart infection that laid him low in 1969. Apparently the trouble was caused by some decayed fragments of teeth left behind after extractions. Now on the mend and at home again, he will have to take it easy for a while but we look forward to seeing his familiar figure, stopwatch in hand, on the finish lines this summer. One thing that cheered him enormously during his incarceration was the sight on TV of Ernest Obeng bearing a Belgrave Club Honours Badge to the 60 metre finish line at Cosford ahead of Allan Wells.

Our already busy General Hon. Secretary Derek Crookes was elected Secretary of the South of the Thames Cross Country Association at their AGM in October. He is obviously doing so well on the Surrey County Committee that his fame is spreading.

An interested spectator at the Autumnal '5¾' was Charlie Smart and it was good to see him chatting away with old friends. Happily he still has some mobility and the fighting spirit which used to strike terror into our old rivals on the Brighton Relay is still evident by the way he tackled the stairs for welcome refreshment at Belgrave Hall. He was the darling of the crowds at the White City - they seemed to think that the balding Belgravian who was carving his way through the field was old enough to be the father of the others! Let's hope we see more of you, Charlie.

In the 1978 Belgrave Draw, organised by Ron Langheim, there was a healthy profit of £275.18 for the Club coffers - £100 up on last year. Thanks and well done Ron!

We hear that Bernard Eglington pulled off the biggest fiddle of his athletic career in October. He has been walking second-claim with Lancs. W.C. for about seven years and had twice won their "Alison Trophy" for a 10 kilometre handicap. When he turned up to compete on October 14th he was astounded to find only officials and himself there. Someone had blundered and no other walkers had turned up. Although he was all for postponing the race the officials insisted that he should set out on his own - which he did - to win the cup for the third time.

One way of getting your name into the Club's minutes is to change your address and one change recently notified was Dick Towndrow who has moved from one address in Mere, Wiltshire, to another in that delightful village. Dick was a member of the old Ashcombe AC, and when they disbanded (they used to run in Richmond Park from Sheen) he came to us via the Poly. During Army service in the war he was stationed at Gillingham, Dorset, and married a local girl. Why mention this? - Some years later a lad from Gillingham came to London to seek fame and fortune and, amongst other things, joined Belgrave - his name - Carl Lawton. Dick was a fine cross-country and road runner and on one occasion won the now discontinued Wigmore '15'. Some years ago he left London to take up a teaching job in Wiltshire.

The Southern Counties Cross Country Association have taken advantage of the tendencies of that compulsive committee member Derek Crookes, our General Hon. Secretary now being elected to that august body's committee.

Good news for speedy tipplers! Haigs, distillers of fine whisky and sponsors of our Belgrave Road Relay (April 7th), have upped the size of the team prizes. In the past the first team has received a 1 gallon bottle of the 'hard stuff', second team half a gallon and third team one quarter of a gallon. This has done nothing to slow down clubs like Aldershot & Farnham and Thames Valley H, so let's see what the new measures can do - first team to receive one whole bottle each, second team half a bottle each and third team quarter of a bottle each.

Congratulations to Doug. Fotheringham on being elected President of the Southern Area of the Race Walking Association. He has been walking for a quarter of a century and was a regular in our "Garnet" Cup teams until he scored in our winning team in 1977 to gain "senior" status. One of his greatest performances was in the 100 miles race promoted by the M.P.A.A. at Chigwell in 1965 when he covered the distance in the fine time of 21hrs. 31mins. 9secs. to become Centurion No. 373. More recently he has been Race Hon. Sec. for the popular M.P.A.A. Open 11 kilos. (formerly 7 miles) held from Imber Court.

John Thresher has joined the ranks of the marathoners. Now 39 years old he lined up in a field of 205 at Regina, Saskatchewan, and finished 5th in 2hrs. 39mins. 25secs. Great stuff John! As a vet in 1980 he says he will be looking for Gorman and trying to avoid O'Hara. John has now moved to Winnipeg and we wish him, Mavis and their children the best of luck in their new home. If anyone wishes to write to John his new address is 238 Oxford Street, Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada. Incidentally, John is still our Club Record holder for 1,500 metres and 1 mile with 3:44.6 and 4:02.1, dating from 1968 and 1964 respectively.

We note that John Blair-Fish, now representing Edinburgh, was 37th in the Barnsley Marathon in 2hrs. 40mins. 22secs. There were 282 finishers.

Poor old Charlie Speechley! At 91 years of age he was competing in the Highgate One Hour Walks, we hear, when someone had the nerve to disqualify him. He was most disappointed and is now said to be thinking of changing his style.

Belated congratulations to two Belgravians who have taken the marital plunge. Howard Satchell (can he really be 20 years a member) has married Chris from Canada, and Arnold Bentt has married Pat. Best wishes to them all.

In November Derek Crookes did not get voted onto the committee of any athletic organisation. When asked by our correspondent what she thought about Derek's "failure", Mrs. Mary Crookes replied, "Who is Derek Crookes?"

It was good to see Len Marchant at the A.G.M. A Club stalwart of the 30's and 40's and a great middle-distance runner who has represented the A.A.A. (regarded by many as the stepping stone to an International Vest). He would probably have been at his best during World War II, when he served in the R.A.F. and picked us up many members. He was a good cross-country and road relay runner and on one occasion was second in the South of the Thames Junior - the winner being Bill Lucas.

GRAPEVINE continued .....

An absentee from the A.G.M. was Frank Webb who has recently undergone an operation. However, you can't keep chaps like Frank away for long and it was good to see him at the '5¾' run.

The Chief Judge at the Chippenham to Calne Walk was George Bentley now living at Portishead, Avon. He looked fit and well and told us that his brother Fred, one of our great long-distance walkers of the 30's and an international in 1938, was also fit and well. Also at the race was Percy Wright who is busy planning the English Schools Road Walking Championships due to be held in Southampton. We hope that many of our younger walkers will be there competing for their counties.

A steering committee was formed in January by the London Borough of Merton to discuss the setting up of a Merton Sports Council. It is not yet resolved whether "steering committees" are allowed to count towards a record attempt but if so, Derek Crookes now needs only one more committee for a World Record and his own niche in the Guiness Book of Records!

Fame at last. Peter Hardwick and Alan Painter were featured on the front page of "Athletics Weekly" for March 10th. Well, perhaps featured is overdoing it a bit, just their rear views being shown along with many other rear views tackling a hill in the 1978 National.

One sees some funny snippets of information around. According to the financial columns "for the six months to July 31st the turnover of Belgrave (Blackheath) turned in at £1.39 million ..... Taxable profit for the last full year was £198,630." Does John Baker know something we don't?
Or what about this one from the "AW": "Tiretta - removes unwanted hair from legs and body-assisting massage. An incredible discovery that acts quickly. No pain or smell, no hours of effort. Send now for this incredible hair remover ... to BELGRAVE DIRECT SUPPLIES LTD, Leicester!"

items.heading: TAPE MEASURES RULE!
items.summary: Article reprinted from "Sport In The USSR" on laser and optical measuring devices in field events and the rule that world records must still be measured with a tape measure.
items.text:
TAPE MEASURES RULE! (from "Sport In The USSR)

In recent years science has provided sportsmen and trainers with a huge variety of technical gadgetry to help them hone their skills by flawlessly registering times. Competing with the noble tape measure are the latest technical devices, which make it possible to register information with degrees of precision which at the present are not even all that necessary. The tape measure is not always laid and stretched evenly, and is affected by temperature. Of course, its influence is not great enough to really affect the measuring of javelin or discus throws, but it does exist. Optical devices measure this distance with mathematical precision.

This type of equipment was first used at the Olympic Games in Munich. The unusual-looking device was reminiscent of a movie camera sitting on a tripod. The official went over to the javelin, which had left a mark in the grass, stuck a reflector into the ground, and the scoreboard would light up, indicating the result. The work here is being done by a laser. An electronic optical tachometer makes it possible to measure simultaneously horizontal distance, curves and a host of other parameters.

Of course no one forbids the use of optic laser devices at sports competitions. Curiously enough, however, they can be utilised only until a world record is set. In this case something rather comical takes place: the judges run for the tape measure and "check" the result measured by a laser device. As of now, the rules prohibit the registering of world records with anything other than a tape measure

items.heading: HARRY HATHWAY
items.summary: Cecil Gittins's obituary of Harry Hathway, the country's leading athletics timekeeper for some twenty years, who died after helping at a meeting.
items.text:
HARRY HATHWAY

A few weeks ago, as I understand it, Harry was (as so very often) helping out at an athletic event, and he felt not too good. Well, the weather had not been kind and Harry was in his seventies. When he was at home that evening he collapsed and when medical help arrived he was dead.

Harry had been the country's top timekeeper for a long, long time - twenty years to my recollection. It was he who developed, organised and arranged proper testing for timekeepers - and those who have read his articles will appreciate the immaculate detail and assembly of factual data which backed up his plans. As an unsure novice timekeeper myself, he was one of those who gave me instruction and encouragement and for that I am grateful. Harry was always firmly and quietly confident in himself but never bombastic; indeed he was always willing to listen to what someone else had to say.

Harry was always around with his multitude of watches at the top internationals but he never neglected the "small" meetings which are the basis of our sport. He was to be seen at Belgrave events often.

He was a retired mathematics teacher and a bachelor, as well as a Roman Catholic of deep conviction. The timekeepers' stand will not be quite the same without Harry.

Cecil Gittins

OCTOBER 7th 1978 - WIMBLEDON.

The Yacht Handicap

As always a scorching hot day was arranged for this popular event over "the usual course" - out to the Windmill and back over the Common. With 46 starters including some notable track stars not usually associated with tarmac and mud it was bound to be another enjoyable race.

The Hon. Handicapper again did a good job managing to get 34 finishers inside 2 minutes of the winner! Although so many were close, the first two were well clear of the rest of the field. items.heading: A NIGHT OUT FOR JOE
items.summary: Account of the gathering at Belgrave Hall on 3 November 1978 where Tom Carter presented Joe McDonald with a plaque for forty years' membership.
items.text:
A NIGHT OUT FOR JOE

Our well known and popular member, Joe McDonald, recently completed forty years membership of the Club, and there was a fine article about him in a recent "Belgravian". To celebrate the occasion a number of his Club friends gathered in Belgrave Hall on Friday, November 3rd for a "get together". A few old Club photographs in which Joe appeared where on display.

Highlight of the evening was the presentation of a plaque, suitably inscribed and complete with the Club Badge. The inscription read:

Presented to
Joe McDonald
by
Belgrave Harriers
In recognition of
40 Years Valued Service
2nd Nov. 1978

The presentation was made by Past President and former cross-country international Tom Carter who, in a witty speech, fittingly short enough for the occasion, paid tribute to Joe's fighting spirit as a member of Club teams for many years and for the unsung but greatly appreciated work he does regularly behind the scenes to help keep Belgrave Hall in good shape.

Joe gratefully accepted the plaque with his usual modesty and to the applause of the gathering of members. Our President was unable to be present but he sent a cordial message which was read out. Everybody will join Ray in wishing him many more years of running and good fellowship with the Club which means so much to Joe.

items.heading: Milton Keynes to host 'Friendly Games'?
items.summary: Note, from the Road Runners Club newsletter, on Milton Keynes' plans for a traffic-free marathon course and stadium and its intended bid for the 1986 Commonwealth Games.
items.text:
Milton Keynes to host 'Friendly Games'?

It was interesting to learn through the Road Runners Club newsletter for January 1979 that the town of Milton Keynes, fast becoming the home of road running and walking in this country, hopes to construct a permanent marathon course which will be completely traffic free and available for use by walkers, runners and joggers, for racing and training. The course will probably consist of a three lap circuit with the start and finish in the 30,000 spectator stadium also planned by the Milton Keynes Development Council. Such items as permanent distance markers, water hydrants and telephones at intermediate points have been discussed, as well as facilities for spectating.

With an indoor sports complex already existing and a plan for an Olympic sized swimming pool on the drawing board, Milton Keynes intends to make a bid for the 1986 Commonwealth Games - last held in England in 1934. Good luck to them.

items.text:
DECEMBER 2nd 1978 - WIMBLEDON - THE 7 MILE C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP.

The Master Mastered

Thirtyseven foolhardy runners braved the December weather and three laps of the Common for this year's Club '7'. After a fast start the front of the field soon split up, led by last year's rivals Ian Duncan and Laurie O'Hara - meeting for the first time this season. Jim Rimmer was the only one to go with the two leaders but he was dropped after one lap and remained isolated in 3rd place. The second group of Gerry North, Lionel Mann, Colin Pearson and Simon Holmes were always falling back and the experience and fitness of Pat O'Connor and Tony Binda brought them through well at the end.

Meanwhile, up at the front, battle was under weigh between the two 'big' names. It seems Ian has been doing some hard training away from the Club this year as he pushed the pace along at the front. The two were still together after one lap but by the halfway mark Ian had forced a gap of about ten metres which he extended over the third lap to finish 35 seconds ahead of Laurie. So we have a new name on the cup at last!

The handicap was won by a much improved Dave Searle with Alan Painter, recovered from his marathon, in 2nd. Mr. Handicapper was fooled by Ian Duncan's absence and the race winner collected his second prize of the day in 3rd place.

DECEMBER 9th 1978 - EPSOM - SURREY C.C. LEAGUE RACE 3.

370 Points Adrift

Belgrave's league fortunes were mirrored by the weather at this third race of the season on a bleak, windy day at Epsom. We needed a miracle to keep alive any hope of staying in division one but it was not to be. Once again we were unable to field our strongest team and never looked like being able to score well enough to improve our position.

After a fast downhill start Jim Rimmer led the Belgrave team followed by Alan Black, Leo Coy, Simon Holmes and Tom Dowdall - having a real 'blinder'. Pat O'Connor, getting fitter every week, was moving through well and at the end of the lap took over from Jim as first scorer. We were packing well but about 30 places too low. On the second lap Tom Dowdall began to 'die' but the thought of beating Gorman kept him going. John Jackson was gradually working through and Simon Holmes moved up into 3rd scoring position ahead of Alan Black. At the end we were last team and overall tailed Herne Hill H by some 370 points with one race left.

JANUARY 6th 1979 - LLOYD PARK.- SURREY COUNTY 7½ MILES C.C. CHAMP.

County Championships

Lloyd Park on a good day is a difficult course - so three laps on a day with a biting wind and several inches of snow was no-ones idea of fun. However, our team was strengthened by the presence of John Abberton, John Bicourt and Simon Williamson and a better result than that in previous league races was hoped for. Our scoring six were soon apparent and although Bicourt and Rimmer were struggling in the snow, Abberton, O'Connor, Williamson and Holmes were running to form and we were packing inside 50. Abberton and Bicourt were always our first two, with the former getting home just 2 seconds ahead to score in 24th place. The other four seemed to be having a private race. Williamson led them through the first lap but once more O'Connor's experience showed as he came through on the second to be our third scorer in 37th. Holmes and Rimmer closed up on Williamson on the second lap but he kept going well and drew away on the last circuit.

Further down the field Tom Dowdall proved his earlier victory over Brian Gorman was no fluke - but only by 2 seconds. Leo Coy seems to be having a rough patch at the moment but no doubt is holding back for the big races later in the season.

items.heading: Duncan's Double
items.summary: Report and results of the club 10 miles cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common on 13 January 1979, Ian Duncan's second club title win of the season ahead of Laurie O'Hara and Jim Rimmer, who won the handicap; with photos of the medallists.

JANUARY 13th 1979 - WIMBLEDON - THE 10 MILES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP.

Duncan's Double

Thirty Belgravians set off over the Common for this year's '10' but only two-thirds lasted the full four laps. The horse-rides, notoriously muddy after rain, were rock hard and caused several people to retire 'hurt'. The rivalry begun in the '7½' before Christmas continued over four laps as Duncan, O'Hara and Rimmer were joined by Williamson and soon broke away from the rest of the field. Ian Duncan looked as though he might pull away early on but suffered a bad fall and did not make his move until the third lap. By this time he and O'Hara had opened up a clear lead over Rimmer and Williamson who had started too fast and struggled to hang on for the second half of the race. Duncan now put on the pressure and got away from Laurie O'Hara to record his second win of the season. By now the rest of the field was well spread out - 4th placed Williamson finished over two minutes up on Lionel Mann in 5th and making a return to form over the longer distance. Leo Coy's training started to pay off as he finished 6th ahead of newcomer (!) Steve Williams having his first race for two months.

The handicapper was seen surveying the scene with pleasure (glad he wasn't running perhaps!) and even pacing Peter Hardwick over the last lap while retrieving the flags!!

The summer should bring some exciting sprint results from our Club Record holder Ernest Obeng if his 'winter' form is anything to go by. items.heading: O'Connor Undaunted By Icy Conditions
items.summary: Report and results of the South of Thames senior cross-country race at Aldershot on 27 January 1979, run on ice and snow, where Pat O'Connor (54th) was Belgrave's best and the team was 16th.
items.text:
JANUARY 27th 1979 - ALDERSHOT - SOUTH OF THAMES 'SENIOR'.

O'Connor Undaunted By Icy Conditions

With the weather continuing to be icy it was not surprising that only eight hardy Belgravians made the trip to Aldershot for this race; and all eight fervently wished that they hadn't bothered. The course was treacherously covered with ice and snow, and the ruts became worse as the race went on. The course was similar to that used in the Surrey league race only longer - about four times as long it seemed!

Even the support of several of our officials could not raise the team and everyone had a "bad one" except Pat O'Connor who once again showed his form over the country by finishing 54th, two places ahead of last year and easily our best man of the day.

Unfortunately the rest of the report is a tale of woe. Tony Binda was forced to stop and walk on the second lap with bad cramp in the stomach and Steve Williams, after a promising return in the '10', was forced to retire with the same diaphragm trouble that has dogged him since the summer. FEBRUARY 10th 1979 - PARLIAMENT HILL - SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C. CHAMPS.

The 'Southern'

After the South of Thames, two weeks before, we thought we had experienced the worst of the weather and conditions but it was not to be. Parliament Hill has always been difficult and it was made doubly so this year by a bitterly cold wind and no changing accommodation! Some people had come changed but for the rest, dressing rooms were either the back seats of cars or out in the open. Nevertheless we managed to field a full team if not our strongest. It was also good to see an old friend in the person of John Stow, unfortunately for us wearing the colours of Woodford Green over his claret and gold.

As usual the mass start up the hill was fast and Belgrave were soon prominent towards the back of the field. As the race wore on ... and on ... Pat O'Connor worked through steadily and passed Stow on the final circuit of the 9 mile course to finish 138th. Simon Holmes was also working through the field but was unable to make the first 200 finishers. Behind him but another 100 places back Lionel Mann ran steadily and only just got home in front of Colin Pearson, having a real 'blinder'. The scoring team was completed by Doug Maugnan, also having a good one and Brian Gorman.

The only enjoyable thing about the afternoon was the warming tea and coffee dispensed at very little charge by Messrs. Carter and Biscoe - once more braving the weather to support the runners.

items.heading: Here We Go Again
items.summary: Report and results of Surrey Cross Country League race 4 at Coulsdon on 17 February 1979, Belgrave's best of the season but too late to avoid relegation, with the final division one table showing Belgrave last.
items.text:
FEBRUARY 17th 1979 - COULSDON - SURREY C.C. LEAGUE RACE 4.

Here We Go Again

The final league race of the year was run over three laps of a shortened Coulsdon course due to the snow and ice still covering the ground. Although certain to be relegated we managed to field one of our strongest teams this year - something we should have done in the first three races. There were some notable absences but those who braved the cold weather ran well and we salvaged some pride by beating Herne Hill by 60 points on the day.

Ian Duncan took over from Pat O'Connor as our leading runner; he was well up the field for the whole race and finished 13th. Simon Holmes was our second scorer for most of the race but was tiring at the end and O'Connor, timing his run to perfection, just got home in front. The deep snow was making the course very slippery and Dennis Brown was further hampered by heavy shoes. He gradually worked through though (encouraging the rest of the team as he went!) and finished just inside the first forty.

With four in forty and our next six evenly spread out up to 78th we scored better than in any of the previous races - but all too late. Next year will see us in Division 2 for the second time in three years - not a happy record and one which we must reverse next season.

Once again our thanks to Gordon Biscoe for his untiring efforts as team secretary. It is doubted that we would even be in Division 2 if not for his work and encouragement.

MARCH 3rd 1979 - STOPSLEY PARK, LUTON - E.C.C.U. CHAMPIONSHIP.

With a record number of 1,672 starters, 1,555 of whom managed to complete the windswept course, it is becoming quite a challenge to finish in the first 1,000. Up front spectators were treated to one of the finest finishes ever with the result in doubt until Elswick's Mike McLeod burst away from Ford (Aldershot), Rose (Bristol) and Kenyon (Bolton) with only 150 metres to go. As far as Belgrave were concerned however, it was one of those "if only" races. If only Laurie O'Hara and Jim Rimmer could have made it... if only Dennis Brown, who was there, was qualified to run.... if only John Bicourt could have finished (he was 17th last year) .... if only Simon Williamson, running well but for Birmingham University as an individual, had been on our team .... our team score would have been about 1,600 points less and our position about 30th instead of 68th. items.heading: from the Belgravian ... 25 years ago
items.summary: Look-back column recalling Ron Linstead's course-record win in the 1954 5¾ mile road race, Belgrave's team win in the 1954 National 20 miles walk, and the club's victory in the 1939 National Cross Country Championship at Manchester.
items.text:
from the Belgravian ... ... 25 years ago

The 5¾ mile road race ..... 27th March 1954 ..... Over 40 runners turned out and there was a surprise winner in Ron Linstead. His time of 28mins. 25secs. was a new course record and once his National Service training is finished he will prove a handful to the best in the country. Charlie Smart who is now back in England for good - we hope - finished 2nd, with John Bromley 3rd.
(Editor's note: Ron was a Youth when winning this race in 1954).

The National 20 miles Walking Championship ..... May 8th 1954 ..... The Championship was held at Birmingham this year and what a grand day it turned out to be for the Club. Once again we are holders of a National title and it was grand to see in a weekly paper "Belgrave National Champions". Our heartiest congratulations to all, particularly George Checkley (9th) who celebrated his birthday by gaining his honours badge. Bernard Eglington (13th) missed his by one position. George Beecham (17th) gained his first National winning team medal, Hugh McGreechan (4th) the Sidney Bayliss Cup.

... and 40 years ago

The National Cross Country Championship 1939 ..... As we go to press comes wonderful news of the winning of the English Cross Country Championship at Manchester ..... 43 teams lined up for the start. Our lads were reasonably well away and at 1½ miles Stimpson and Penny were near the leaders, with our other runners well placed. At three miles the same state of affairs existed, but the large field passing in a solid mass of mud and humanity, with the rain pouring down, prevented any very definite conclusions being drawn. We knew that both Birchfield and ourselves were doing well..... On the next lap (5.3 miles) rough calculations showed us to be leading by a few points from Birchfield. Our runners were advised of this and seemed to run with more determination than ever. As they came round again (7.6 miles) to start the last lap we still led, but the Birchfield crowd were urging their team to gain positions.

Then to the finish to await the arrival of the runners. First home was Jack Holden, of Tipton H., a worthy winner. Our first man home was Ted Stimpson, in fourth position, scoring 3 for team purposes. He had improved from 14th to 4th position over the last lap of 2.3 miles, passing seasoned runners as though they were not in the race. His effort was an amazing one, and our team had an excellent start. Then came Arthur Penny (5), another to rise to the occasion on an awful day. A few seconds delay and Tom Carter (17) appeared, followed a little later by our Captain, Bert Footer (28), who had gained place after place in the second half of the race.

We now wanted two others to complete our team, and three claret and gold vests came along together. Harry Shields (34) and Dan Patience (35) managed to catch and beat A.W.Jerman on the run-in, and we had won the "National" for the second time!

items.heading: WITH THE LADIES
items.summary: Ray Hall's ladies' section column on Sunday training at Battersea Park, promotion in the Lily 'B' League, coming Southern League and GRE Cup fixtures, the ladies' cross-country season, coaching lectures by Bruce Longden, injured members and thanks to helpers, with photos of captains Dawn McNeil and Wendy Dunsford.
items.text:
WITH THE LADIES

There was a young lady named Bright,
Whose speed was faster than light,
She set out one day
In a relative way,
And returned home the previous night.

Sorry to inform you but we've no ladies called Bright. But I can promise you some fine sprinting from the ladies section during the coming season thanks to the training that takes place every Sunday morning at Battersea Park under the direction of that task-master Frank Simmons.

It gladdens my heart (yes I do have one) when I arrive to find 25 young athletes waiting to start training. If you have not been to Battersea Park lately, it is still bloody cold, wet and depressing but in winter twice as bad. During the winter the numbers have been surprising considering the weather conditions and in spite of the amount of hard work done the previous week, the girls still come back for more.

reports by Ray Hall

With the track season coming up fast, we look forward with anticipation to the Girls and Juniors facing stronger opposition in Lily 'B' Division II after our sensational win in the last match of 1978 where the result gave us second place by 2 points - Belgrave 949 and Dorking St. Paul's 947. So we were finally promoted with Aldershot & Farnham. The only complaint was from the Aldershot Team Manager who stated, "Oh! no. I've not got your noisy lot again." Sorry but yes you have.

The Lily 'B' League has been extended to four matches for this season and all these matches are away - Croydon, Guildford, Aldershot and Woking. In the Womens' Southern League our journeying is short - to Dartford, Bexley and a home match at Battersea Park where competition will come from Dartford, Bexley Borough, Havant and Hercules Wimbledon.

For the Southern League our two Captains Dawn McNeil (Track) and Wendy Dunsford (Field) will select the teams to take some of the work off my shoulders. Also, for the first time, we have entered the Womens' GRE Cup, and our first round match is at Croydon on Sunday May 6th. This competition is for Seniors only. Other matches have been arranged at Dorking and Woking but the trip to Hastings could not be accepted because of clashing with other fixtures.
WE NEED YOUR SUPPORT FOR ALL THESE FIXTURES.......................

The cross-country season has not brought any outstanding athletes to light wearing Belgrave vests. We have competed in the new cross country league but the support on the whole has been disappointing. The best sections have been the 'Inters' and Seniors, ably led by Pam Davies whose age I will not reveal (her children are great company). The supporting team has been made up of joggers, shot putters and some whose events have not yet been classified. At the time of writing, after three matches, they lead with 11 points from Croydon and Surrey Beagles, both 8 points. In the other two sections Girls and Juniors, we are bottom but Alison Jones, Tina Jordon and Joanne Warnett have enjoyed the experience.

In the County Cross Country Championships, Alison Jones had a tough race in the Middlesex event at Ruislip and Tina Jordon ran at Dorking in the "Surreys". I hope next year, perhaps, we will have a team competing.

In the coaching area we arranged three lectures by Bruce Longden (Daley Thompson's coach). We all enjoyed the first on Sprinting and Relay racing but the second was cancelled because of the weather. Its a disgrace that in a club of our size this is possibly the first effort in this area for many years. We look forward to the Hurdles lecture with the Guy Drut film. Perhaps someone will answer the question: "Why is it that Belgrave is so far behind in coaching and why it needs so much work and thought to bring it up to date?" With some effort we could motor to the elite of British athletic clubs so please put down your history books and give us all the help you can.

Invalids:

Pleased to hear that the diminutive Mary McPartlin is getting better after a serious illness and we look forward to seeing her competing in the Lily B matches in the summer.

Valerie Bridges' back injury is slowly getting better and we are pleased to see Rebecca Augustin training after the operation on her leg.

Gordon Doubleday, our timekeeper, has spent six weeks in hospital getting his own "ticker" seen to. We hope his recovery is speedy and that he too will soon be in action again.

Thanks:

To Carl Lawton for all his good work with the women walkers, and congratulations for the first set of W.C.C. & R.W.A. National medals for 3rd team. Well done Linda Nicholls for winning the Southern "Inter" title, and Shirley Rook and Anna Matthews for 2nd and 3rd in the Southern Senior race in the snow.

To Frank Simmons for all his work on Sundays at Battersea Park. After seeing the training you can understand why he gets no "valentines". Those two eyes see everything on the track.

To Ian Jones and Ken Jordon for their support and encouragement during the winter.

To Ted Weldin and Richard Dorman at the C.C. League and last but not least my Assistant Derek Jones, who is always there, even during the difficult personal times he's had lately.

If I've forgotten anybody - sorry!

items.heading: JACK BIDGOOD M.B.E.
items.summary: Obituary of Jack Bidgood MBE, Metropolitan Police chief superintendent and Belgrave walker who won the 1950 Barking to Southend walk and chaired the Southern R.W.A.
items.text:
JACK BIDGOOD M.B.E.

We were sorry to learn that Jack Bidgood died early in December; he must have been well into his seventies. He was born and brought up in Devon and followed the normal sporting life of a Devonian. Later he came to London and joined the Metropolitan Police where he became interested in walking and joined Belgrave. This was in our days of walking supremacy and he figured in many of our teams in National Championships (20 miles and 50 kilos only in those days), the London to Brighton and many provincial walks. As a policeman he was, of course, a regular competitor in the Barking to Southend Walk which he won in 1950. He also won the Club's Long-Distance Championship - held in conjunction with the London to Brighton Walk.

Obviously then a great performer himself, he was always ready to give advice and encouragement to newcomers to the sport. He also found time to help on the administrative side and served a term of office as Chairman of the Southern R.W.A. During this period of office the Southern Committee decided to launch a magazine for walkers only - "Race Walking Record". Remembering that this was in World War Two it was a brave decision. After retiring from the active side he was a Judge for many years.

He had a great career in the Metropolitan Police, finishing with the rank of Chief Superintendent. He was awarded the M.B.E. for meritorious service to the Force.

Volumes could be written about his personality. He did much to foster the idea that the off-duty policeman could be as good a club man as any. He insisted that whilst engaged in sport he was called Jack - and Jack he was to everybody. He was as likeable and as pleasant a fellow as one could wish to meet.

He had suffered indifferent health over the last few years, but his passing came as a surprise. We say farewell to a fine character who not only set an example by his sportsmanship but was a stalwart friend.

G.S.D.

items.heading: WALKING
items.summary: Walking Secretary Carl Lawton's review of the walking season: rising numbers, the Juniors' National 10 kilometres team win, the girls' team prizes, John Newnham's comeback, individual honours, the finances of the club's Open 7 mile walk, and plans for a training camp and more out-of-London races.
items.text:
WALKING

A few seasons ago the walking editorial queried "where have all the walkers gone?". Since that time there has been a promising upturn in our numbers and as a result the allocation of National numbers issued to Belgrave has almost been used up.

Results have, on the whole, been very good since the previous issue of the magazine and turn-outs for races have improved though we seldom manage that magical 100% - a feat we did achieve in the National J/Y/B at Coventry. On studying the results it will be seen that we have not been having to rely on the basic four as some clubs do. In fact in the four "opens": Chippenham, Vauxhall, Enfield and Belgrave, no less than ten permutated to pick up team prizes. In addition to that another eight have appeared in placed teams in recent months. It has on certain occasions given the Secretary problems in deciding who to put into the 'A' team.

Although we did not win a Senior National title last year the Juniors did their bit by winning the 10 kilometres. The second time in three years that we have won it and as a result congratulations go to Richard Dorman, Paul Blagg and Trevor McDermot and commiserations to the four behind them who, had they walked for other clubs, would have been in the scoring teams. In the Youths we did not do so well but it was not for the lack of trying. We could well have placed 3rd had we not had the misfortune of disqualifications but at least we started a team and congratulations to Mike Nicholls for his 3rd place.

We have had our problems with the Girls this year. With our small numbers it does prove difficult to raise teams on every occasion through work and other reasons but when we have succeeded we have usually come away with a prize: first team at Chippenham and 3rd in the National 5 kilometres. The "National" was a very good performance but had we a full and fit team we could have done far better.

It is rather impractical to mention everyone who has done his or her bit for the Club (it might be easier to mention those who have not) but outstanding this year is undoubtedly John Newnham. Although he dabbled about six years ago and reached the echelons of six miles an hour in the Highgate Hour walks, he decided to have another go last year and much to his own and the Club's suprise has turned into one of the regular team men. He has no secret of success - just dedication.

Others worthy of mention are Paul Blagg, Junior International; Richard Dorman, 2nd in the National Junior; Mike Nicholls, 3rd in the National Youths; Graham Seatter and Allan Callow, Commonwealth Games competitors; Derek Howie, Scottish International; Linda Nicholls, 2nd in the W.A.A.A. Championship. We had County Champions in Graham Seatter, John Hall, Carl Lawton, Richard Dorman, Kevin McDermot, Trevor McDermot, Linda and Mike Nicholls. Derek Ellis was the Police Cadet Champion, Shirley Rook the National Police Champion (for running but she walks mostly) and John Dunsford placed 3rd in the European Veterans Championships.

The Annual Belgrave promotion, the 'Open 7 mile walk', had as most of you know a revised course this year. This was to ease the worsening problem of the traffic around the Common. Generally it proved successful and once again thanks are due to those within the Belgrave circle but not actually members: Joan Goswell, Wyn Cook and Jean Middleton, who do such sterling work. We did have a small problem with pointsmen but that should not happen again. Thanks, in no small way, also go to those who, with their generosity, enable the Club to keep up a high standard of prizes. The cost of prizes last year came to nearly £120, with receipts from entries just £60. Thus another £60 had to be raised to cover the cost of the promotion and much of this came from the prize fund and the rest (total outlay was nearly £160) from teas, programmes and the raffle.

Although very little is done within the Club with regard to coaching for walking, it being carried out on an individual basis, it is anticipated to try and hold a training camp over a long weekend. By the time you read this, plans should be well advanced. In addition it is planned to make more of an impact on races which the Club has not competed in for a while. The turn-out for the Leicester Mercury last year was rather poor so that is a good starting point. There is also the Birmingham 35kms plus possibly a couple of Northern races - the Morecambe 20kms and the Sheffield '15' or the Bradford 50kms. With our strength in depth there is no reason why we should not support more races out of London. If we expect other clubs to come to us we should return the compliment. It is a few years since we won the Leicester Mercury on the Saturday and then placed second in the Bradford event two days later with a completely different team. Two other races to prepare for this year will be the Surrey Walking Club 100 miles at Ewhurst and the inaugural 100 kilometre championship, both of which we should be able to support at full strength.

Carl Lawton Walking Secretary

items.heading: Family Occasion

items.text:
Race reports by Gordon Doubleday

AUGUST 26th 1978 - ENFIELD.

Family Occasion

The Festival of Walking promoted by the Borough of Enfield H. drew a number of us to Enfield and amongst our participants we had three from each of the McDermot and Nicholls families with John Morris and son (Peter) as well.

In the first event we had two Junior Ladies lined up for the 2,500 metres and it was good to see the fine styles (not to mention the enthusiasm) shown by the youngest members of the two families. They are both also keen swimmers.

There were three teams contesting the Youths' 5,000m and with Mike walking strongly for 2nd place, well supported by Kevin and Peter, we took first team awards, scoring 10 points to the 14 of Waltham Forest. The Havering team failed to close in.

About five minutes after the start of the Youths, the Senior Ladies started over the same course. Anna walked confidently all the way to finish 4th, followed home by a fast finishing Linda. With a fighting performance by Jane we gained another "first" scoring 12 points to beat Epsom & Ewell H 15, and Brighton & Hove 19.

The "big'un", 20 kilometres over a six lap course, showed us to be without some of our top performers but our team gave a good account of themselves to finish a close 4th, the scoring being Ilford 36, Enfield 37, Brighton & Hove 37 and Belgrave 40. The hero of the race was Richard Dorman, walking his second 20kms. He was near to the leaders right from the start and a well judged performance gave him 7th place, 46 seconds over the 100 minute "barrier". Examination of the result sheet showed Richard to be ahead of several good men. Our next man was John Newnham who continues to make his presence felt - he deserved a team prize and his turn will surely come. Not far behind came the other John (Dunsford) - 1st Veteran home. Making his debut over the distance was Trevor McDermot who walked the first half with Ray and then showed us what a prospect he is by dropping Ray (his second 10kms was faster than his first), to get under 110 minutes. Our other walkers no doubt preferred the sunshine to the drenching they got last year!

Keep a lookout for further references to the McDermots and Nicholls - these two walking families are surely going to grace our pages for many years.

items.heading: SEPTEMBER 2nd 1978 - LONDON TO BRIGHTON
items.summary: Walking report on the 1978 London to Brighton walk, where Belgrave failed to start a team for the first time but Dave King and John Keown finished 18th and 26th; part of Gordon Doubleday's race reports series begun on page 40.
items.text:
SEPTEMBER 2nd 1978 - LONDON TO BRIGHTON

For the first time in the Club's history we failed to start a team in the London to Brighton walk. We had the minimum of four entered and when Ron Day announced his unfitness to walk owing to injury John Hall decided not to start. This left our two evergreen stalwarts Dave King and John Keown to carry our colours down this famous road. This they did to good effect, finishing 18th in 9:34:24 and 26th in 9:54:54.

Our other starter, Derek Howie, entered as an individual, put up a plucky performance for his first "Brighton". For well over half way he was always near the leaders but over the last miles he began to lose places and became unsteady so wisely retired with just nine miles left. He was full of praise for his attendant Richard Dorman, escorting him by cycle, who had endeavoured to keep him going.

One "regular" we missed was John Morris who was unfit. However, he didn't deny us for he soon came through the field on his motor-cycle, with Peter on the back, to help our pair along. Another motor-cyclist was Joe Coleman, a regular on the Judges Panel for this event.

It was good to see Charlie Speechley at the finish - "Dr. Brighton" obviously plays a part in keeping him 90 years young!

MORRIS DANCES TO FIFTH COLNBROOK TITLE.

John Morris, Belgrave's stalwart long distance walker, showed that he is still a force to be reckoned with when in December he regained the Colnbrook long distance walk championship in 2 hours 21 minutes 34 seconds. John, who has now notched up five wins, although he has not won for the last four years, threw off an early challenge to win convincingly by five minutes to show that he is still in with a chance in this year's long distance events.

items.heading: Giant's View
items.summary: Report of Carl Lawton winning the South Western Counties Open 20km walk at Cerne Abbas on 17 September 1978, with Belgrave taking the team race.
items.text:
SEPTEMBER 17th 1978 - CERNE ABBAS - SOUTH WESTERN COUNTIES OPEN 20K.

Giant's View

One of the sights of the village of Cerne Abbas, Dorset, is the giant carved out of the turf of the surrounding hills. He must have looked down upon generations of pedestrians but none can have moved faster than Carl did when winning the S.W. Counties Open 20 Kilos over a four lap course. Twenty-odd walkers completed the tough course on a warm, sunny day. Various local championships were incorporated in the event but our interest was in the open team race where the opposition came from S.W. clubs.

Carl led from the start and gave a fine exhibition of walking to win in 98 minutes 6 seconds, splendid considering the severity of the course. Getting back into form was Len whose crisp style is beginning to bite again. Bob and John fought it out for three laps but Bob proved stronger over the last lap to complete the winning team. John, a newcomer, stuck it out bravely - he won't find many courses as hilly.

A handicap showed Len 2nd (he also took the Vet's prize) and Bob 3rd. Once again there was a warm welcome for us; the high regard in which Belgrave is held all over the country is always most gratifying.

One of Carl's prizes will be a reminder of the Giant - a small model made by local craftsmen from horse-shoe nails, with very realistic detail.

items.heading: Maud Heath's Causeway
items.summary: Report of the Chippenham to Calne 6 miles open road walk on 14 October 1978, where Carl Lawton won for the fifth time, Belgrave won the men's team and the ladies also won their race.
items.text:
OCTOBER 14th 1978 - CHIPPENHAM TO CALNE 6 MILES OPEN ROAD WALK.

Maud Heath's Causeway

Many years ago a lady of this name used to walk with the farm produce to market over the watery meadows in the Calne, Wiltshire, area. She spent her savings on building a road and bridges to ease the journey and there is now a column erected to her memory. Nowadays folk from many parts of the country walk from Chippenham to Calne and untramelled by baskets of eggs etc. no doubt go somewhat faster than did the good lady.

Why all this? After seeing the start of this year's walk I was transported to Calne via the Causeway so as to avoid the heavy traffic at the start. The only part of the race I saw was the finish.

Carl led the team home to notch up his 5th win with 41 seconds to spare. Seventh was Richard Dorman who took the prize for first Junior and four places later came Paul, further evidence of our growing strength in the Junior ranks. Fourth Belgravian to finish was Len but he had been declared in the 'B' team. It wasn't long before John Newnham came in to complete our winning scratch team - with three visits to the prize table it was a day he won't forget! Claret and gold vests came in thick and fast with 10 in the first 35. A great performance by one of the youngest in the race was that of Kevin McDermot, 53rd in a time which indicates that he will soon be under the hour for seven miles. John, Richard, Nigel Morris and Bob Picton won the handicap team award with a total time over six minutes better than the second team. John and Richard also took individual handicap awards.

Walking the same course the Ladies had their own race. The winner was the diminutive Carol Tyson (Lakeland AC) in an excellent 48:21 - a time which would have given her 12th place in the mens' race! In 5th place, inside the hour, came Shirley - walk or run she always gives a good performance. Bang on the hour came Linda, having a spot of muscle trouble. Jane put up her usual supporting performance, one of her best, finishing in front of the second and third scorers of the other teams - another sterling win for our ladies.

As if this wasn't enough, when the raffle was drawn Linda's number came out first. Just like old times with the added pleasure of having the ladies joining in the awards.

I've checked the Causeway on the map - it is indicated and named as such.

When the Mayor of Chippenham, Councillor M. Plumb, spoke at the prize-giving after the Chippenham to Calne Walk he expressed his pleasure at the number going to Belgrave - a club of which he was once a member. He joined us in 1954 or 55 when he was a member of the Aristotle Road School Athletics team which won the South London Schools under 13 trophy. He was a shot putter and was introduced to us by his sportsmaster, Colin Collis. Colin very kindly sent us a photograph of the team and amongst those in it were Alan Black and his twin brother and one or two others who joined us for a while. He trained conscientiously at Battersea Park and Tooting Bec tracks and performed well at his chosen event.

We certainly wish him and the Mayoress every happiness in his term of office, which obviously has its pleasant side when he sees his old club successfully competing down his way.

items.heading: The Open Walk
items.summary: Report and results of the Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon on 25 November 1978, won by Mike Parker of Brighton & Hove with Carl Lawton 2nd and Belgrave 2nd team, plus the first Open Ladies race won by Carol Tyson.
items.text:
NOVEMBER 25th 1978 - WIMBLEDON - BELGRAVE OPEN 7 MILES WALK.

The Open Walk

Once again we were blessed with good weather. The new three lap course was used which involves three times up the "hills" by what must be the steepest route (Cottenham Drive). Our President Ray started the race and then took his place in the field.

The early leader was Mike Parker (Brighton & Hove) with Carl, closely followed by Brian Armstrong (Ilford), leading the rest. It was good to see Derek Howie on one of his trips from Stirling. Unfortunately he developed some leg trouble which proved a drawback - he is having this put right before competing again. Mike Scamell was showing us a taste of what to expect when he becomes eligible to represent us early in the New Year. John Hall was going well as were the younger brigade - Richard, Trevor, Kevin and Mike, plus the steadily improving John Newnham.

Would the sharp pace be blunted by the "hills"? It didn't affect Mike Parker who finished strongly over two minutes ahead of Carl. John, Derek and Richard completed the team to give us 38 points and second place to Brighton & Hove, 31 points. We were closely followed by Surrey WC, 41 points, and it is good to see our old rivals back in the reckoning. Once again our non-scorers were hot on the heels of the team - it is pleasing to note the steady progress of Pete Morris, his name is creeping up the finishing lists. One other Belgravian had to make a trip to the prize table - Doug Fotheringham who took 8th individual handicap prize. The prizes were handed out by our President, Ray, and it was good to see the affection and goodwill which he enjoys amongst the race-walkers.

The first Open Ladies Race to be held in conjunction saw some brilliant walking by Carol Tyson (Lakeland AC), her time would have brought her 29th position in the main race. Unfortunately there were only four starters. Our own Shirley earned applause for her efforts.

The smooth conduct of the race was once again in the hands of Club "Old Faithfuls", and it was pleasing to see Joe Coleman active as Chief Judge. Once again our thanks to the Race Hon. Secretary Carl Lawton who organised things with his usual thoroughness.

items.heading: Shirley's Here !
items.summary: Report and results of the Women's R.W.A. National Walking Championships at Melksham on 3 December 1978, where Shirley Rook, Linda Nicholls and Jane Pritchard won Belgrave's first National team medals in a women's event (3rd team).
items.text:
DECEMBER 3rd 1978 - MELKSHAM, WILTS. - WOMENS R.W.A. NATIONAL CHAMPS.

Shirley's Here !

BELLES WIN THEIR FIRST SET OF NATIONAL MEDALS.

The Womens' C.C. and R.W.A. National Walking Championships were held at Melksham, Wiltshire, on a cold, damp day and when we all met up we were disappointed to discover that we had only two competitors for each of the three events. Anna Matthews had already let us know that she wouldn't be competing and Caroline Khan, who has walked so well on the track, was missing from the 3,000 metres race.

The first race, the under 13 2,500 metres, saw Bernadette Sexton and Tracey Nicholls in action. It was a small field and in spite of their lowly positions they showed what good competitors they are. Their experience should stand them in good stead for the next track season when they should pick up some good points in League fixtures

Well warmed up for the under 15 3,000 metres were Tracey McDermot with brother Kevin in attendance, and Ros. There were some fast movers here and our pair showed what fine performers they are becoming. They came fighting their way through the finish in fine style.

A short walk down the road took us to the start of the Seniors 5,000 metres. The rain was increasing and Linda and Jane, well wrapped up, were keeping warm before being called to the start. Suddenly a voice called out, "Shirley's here" and on looking round we saw a smiling Shirley who had motored down. The Belgrave morale shot up immediately - we had a team after all and they were going to have a go for some medals.

At the start Carol Tyson (Lakeland AC) and evergreen Judy Farr (Trowbridge) were soon leading with many hot on their heels, walking impeccably. Our trio looked lively. With one mile to go Carol was clearly away with three others battling away for the placings. When the rest appeared Shirley was going strongly soon followed by fast moving Linda. Later came Jane, working hard to improve her position.

Carol Tyson won convincingly but there must have been some battle for the placings, Karen Eden (Solihull) and Irene Bateman (Basildon) taking 2nd and 3rd places with Judy Farr 4th. When the "field" came in Shirley soon arrived followed by Linda - both had kept up the pressure over the closing stages to ensure good placings. Jane too had put in some good walking and din't relax until she had crossed the line.

A happy group of Belgravians were at the finish speculating upon the team's position. Some hopefuls said third and this was soon officially confirmed. So, we had won our first set of National Team medals in a Womens' event - the first of many we hope. Congratulations to Shirley, Linda and Jane who made our trip to Melksham a day to remember. One thing which delighted me was the look of joy on the faces of the four who had walked earlier - you would have thought that they had won the medals! - their turn will come.

items.summary: Local-history note on the 1845 experimental railway track of a Mr. Prosser near the Windmill (on the route of the club's Yacht '3' course), with two engravings from the Illustrated London News.
items.text:
COMMON KNOWLEDGE

About halfway between the Kingsmere pond and the Windmill lies the site of an experimental railway track laid down in 1845 to test the invention of a Mr. Prosser. This part of the track was built in a circle but a further straight stretch leading off the circle probably extended well down Windmill Road, along which our Yacht '3' course also travels.

The rails were rectangular in section and made of a chemically hardened wood. The train designed for this track had flangeless wheels but had guiding wheels set at 45° to the horizontal with right angled grooves which engaged the rails. The train was said to be more economic than the "iron railway" due to the lack of friction; the power needed was only about three-quarters of that required for a conventional locomotive.

items.heading: TRIP TO SWEDEN
items.summary: Linda Nicholls describes her three-week walking training holiday with the Swedish club Enhorna I.F. near Stockholm, including a weekend camp and a championship at Boras.
items.text:
Linda Nicholls writes of her

TRIP TO SWEDEN

In September, as a result of an invitation through my family, I travelled to Sweden for a three weeks training holiday. During my stay I trained with the Swedish club Enhorna I.F. They are an extremely pleasant group of people and were very helpful and friendly during the period I was with them.

Their training sessions, usually two evenings a week, are held on the outskirts of Stockholm. The sessions are similar to those at Belgrave Hall but with more emphasis on exercising and sprinting. It was interesting to see that youngsters of eight and nine were training very seriously and walking quite long distances.

At weekends when there were no races there would be a two day camp in the country. I was fortunate in being invited to one of these and it was again noticable that general exercises were a major part of their training. All of the walkers would carry out the same exercises and this would be followed by a long steady stroll over forest paths which are plentiful in that area. The distances covered over the two days were in the region of 25 kms. although the youngsters would only do about half that. Although the training was harder than I have ever done before it was an enjoyable weekend.

There was an excellent club spirit amonst the walkers and Siw Gustavsson, with whom I trained and who is one of the leading Swedish walkers, made me feel very much at home.

I was invited to walk in one of the major championships held at Boras There I found that many eight and nine year olds were racing. In fact there were seventeen different grades of walkers including the leading Finns and Swedes. Regrettably, with so much talent about, I suffered an inferiority complex.

During my three week stay I managed a few trips around Stockholm and saw many of its notable sites, discovering that the city is made up of a number of islands all linked by a number of bridges.

Overall I had an interesting and enjoyable trip and if all goes well I hope to have a reciprocal arrangement next year with some of their walkers coming over here.

items.heading: MOST MERITORIOUS PERFORMANCE ?
items.summary: Tribute to Shirley Rook, 20, who missed the coach to the women's National walk but drove 100 miles to compete and helped Belgrave win its first National team medals.
items.text:
MOST MERITORIOUS PERFORMANCE ?

Imagine having been selected to represent Belgrave in a National only to arrive too late to catch the coach on a 200 mile round trip to compete. Would you have called it a day and gone home and apologised later or would you have done the alternative thing - gone home, got into your car, driven the 100 miles not knowing the exact venue and eventually finding it with minutes to spare? Most would have undoubtedly have settled on the former but Shirley Rook (20),to her credit, did the latter. As a result she helped Belgrave collect their first National Team Medals.

Shirley did more for Belgrave in one day than most of us do in a year.

items.heading: SPOTLIGHT ON - ARNOLD BENTT
items.summary: Alan Mead's profile of Belgrave high jumper, long jumper and pole vaulter Arnold Bentt: his best performances, schools and junior career in the 1960s (UK number one junior high jumper in 1968), his relaxed approach since, and his own view of the sport.
items.text:
SPOTLIGHT ON - ARNOLD BENTT

Five times England Schools competitor 1965-1969.

by Alan Mead

One of the most talented and regular members of the Belgrave track and field team for the last decade and more, Arnold is second to very few other Belgravians when one considers the total number of points he has amassed for the club in League and inter-club matches during that period. Now twenty-eight, he admits that he hasn't really trained hard since he left school.... in fact more than that ....he now rarely trains at all! For Arnold getting fit now means beginning to compete in May, gradually overcoming the sore muscle stage and working up a competition edge as the season wears on.

A typical trophy meeting will see him arrive well after the match has started (when travelling by coach we tell him to get there half an hour before anyone else), go straight into the fourth round of the pole vault (it's always worth declaring him even if he's not there yet), lazily soar over about 3 metres and then start looking round for something else to do.

*   *   *

Arnold was born in 1950 in Kingston, Jamaica, and came to London at the age of nine. He went to St. Gerard's School and by the time he was thirteen was already showing an interest in athletics. "Little Joe" Harvey, now long since fallen by the wayside but then one of Frank Simmons' regulars at the Ravenstone School weight training sessions, introduced Arnold to the Club and he became a member in June, 1963. Before long he was sweating his way round Frank's circuits like the rest of us, being shouted at to "Get your knees up!" and showing his enjoyment of this treatment by coming back for more punishment at Battersea Park track on Sunday mornings.

Third place in the Boys' "Mrs. L. Ryan" Cup marked his entry to competition in 1964, covering thows, jumps and running events from 100 yards to half a mile; the ideal way to start off for a youngster in athletics - having a go at everything. By the following year though, it was obvious that jumping was to be his forte.

From this period on Belgrave Harriers were fortunate in having a remarkable squad of long jumpers training under coach Dave Ansell's supervision: John Mitchell, Cliff Brooks, Bob Jones and later Alan Lerwill and Steve White. It was not surprising that in such a fertile atmosphere and under the careful nurturing of one of the best jumping coaches of the time, Arnold's talent bloomed.

Having won the London Schools long jump in 1965 he went on to place second in the All-England event but "coach" was particularly impressed with his high jumping potential. The "Belgravian" reported that fourteen year old Arnold Bentt had reached 1.72 (5'8") at a time when the top ten juniors in the country ranged from 1.90 (6'3") down to 1.80 (5'11") but Arnold had another four years in hand over many of these top rankers and therefore had excellent prospects of leading the junior lists before reaching senior status. (Seniors were eighteen and over in those days.)

In 1966 Arnold began to be plagued by a heel injury that was to hold back his progress for the next two years. Nevertheless, he took several long and high jump wins in junior trophy meetings, represented London Schools again in the long jump, set youth and junior Club records in the high jump, won his first Club Championship in the junior "high" with a silver medal in the senior event to boot, and even beat Steve White over 100 yards!

He had more or less switched to the high jump full time by 1967, finding that jumping for length continued to pound his injury prone heel. In spite of not really improving his best leap since 1965 his competitive record was good. Retaining the junior Club title, he also annexed the senior event. The Surrey County junior title was added to his list of achievements and he represented Surrey in the Inter-Counties, placed 2nd in the London Schools and made his 3rd trip to the England Schools Championships where he reached 6th. Probably the highlight of the season, however, was his selection to take part in the Inter-Cities match in Denmark where he returned to the long jump.

*   *   *

The big break-through came the following year after concentrating on the technique side of his high jumping. Arnold was always an exponent of the straddle style, particularly admiring the art as executed by Russia's Valeriy Brumel before that man's career was wrecked by a motor-cycling accident. Paradoxically, it was this year, 1968, that the athletics world became introduced to the "Fosbury Flop" when Dick Fosbury (USA) won the Mexico Olympic event with his then unusual but now most common style; but for Arnold the practised discipline of the straddle was the key to his success.

In a leisurely inter-club match at Tootirg he went over 6 feet for the first time. Then came the South London Schools title which he took in his stride at 1.86 (6'1½"), followed by his burst onto the National scene by winning the London event in 1.91 (6'3½") to become the United Kingdom's number one junior (fulfilling the "Belgravian" prediction) - seventh on the senior list. He came into the competi-

continued on following page ...

SPOTLIGHT ON ARNOLD BENTT continued ......

tion late, moving up from 1.82 (6'0") in 2 inch intervals to 1.93 (6'4") before failing at 1.98 (6'6"). It has always mystified him how this jump got written down to 6'3". As it was a record height the officials remeasured it by tape - 6'3½" - but finally it was reported as 6'3". As our senior club record is 1.91 (6'3½") dating back to 1936 one can understand his disappointment.

Other landmarks in 1968 included competing in Strasbourg in the International Catholic Games, "failing" with fifth place and 1.77 (5'10") in the England Schools when the winner leapt only 1.85 (6'1") and retaining both Club high jump titles.

Broadening his horizons and with injury problems overcome, Arnold set personal bests in 1969 in the long jump, 200 metres, and high hurdles, winning the Club Championship in the latter event. Six feet was all that was required of him to take the South London Schools event yet again but in the "London's" he was below form and his final trip to the England Schools was again disappointing with 1.77 (5'10") for sixth place on countback even though he equalled the silver medallists height. Further representative honours came his way when he carried Lambeth's colours in Germany against Vincennes and Castrop Rauxel.

*   *   *

Somehow, Arnold's athletic career failed to move on from this point. Perhaps it was the transition from school to work.....maybe Dave Ansell's subsequent migration to Leeds and the dissolving of our school of jumpers. Maybe it was a little of each of these things but probably the underlying reason is that for Arnold athletics is just not the "be all and end all". Notwithstanding this, he has not missed a season with us since and still pops out a really good performance now and then - witness that 13.99 triple jump a couple of seasons back.

Arnold has dabbled at basketball, training and competing for Wandsworth in the early 70's but his real passion is reading. He avidly devours scientific literature, anything on parapsychology, the forces of nature, fringe medicine, the occult, UFO's; a list of subjects that makes him a most interesting conversationallist.

His team mates mostly see him as a super-relaxed, happy-go-lucky individual but Arnold does not subscribe to this view of himself.

"I suppose I've got a bit of talent and that might make it look casual when I compete but really it is just a matter of what is important to one. To me athletics is not that important. I enjoy it, and I'll carry on as long as I do enjoy it - and anyway, it's good for my physical well-being.

"But I suppose I do miss the times when there was a group of us in the Club all working and training towards a particular group of events. A bit of competition in training, like going round "circuits" in pairs, encourages enthusiasm."

*   *   *

What stupendous performances might we have seen from an Arnold Bentt that trained through the 70's like he did when at school....taking on an ever increasing work load....aiming for the top....? We will never know but anyway, it just wouldn't be Arnold would it?
